items.prompt: Write a 3-sentence narrative with a clear beginning, middle, and end about a time you helped someone. Use at least two temporal words and include how you felt at the end.
items.answer: One day, my little sister was crying because she could not tie her shoes. First, I sat down beside her and showed her how to make two loops. Finally, she did it herself, and I felt so proud that I gave her a big hug.

steps: Beginning: who, when, what problem existed.
Middle: first event with a temporal word.
Ending: result and feeling.

items.prompt:
Read this narrative and identify at least two things to improve. Then rewrite it.

'I played. It was fun. The end.'
items.answer: Problems: no details about who, where, what kind of play; no temporal words; 'The end' is not a real closing sentence. Improved: 'One sunny afternoon, I played soccer with my neighbor at the park. First, we set up goals with our shoes. Then, we kicked the ball back and forth until it got dark. Finally, we walked home tired but laughing, and I could not wait to play again.'

steps: Add details: who played, where, what kind of play.
Add temporal words: First, Then, Finally.
Replace 'The end' with a meaningful closing that shows a feeling or reaction.

items.prompt: Write a 4-sentence imagined narrative about being able to fly for one day. Include a beginning, two events, and an ending with a feeling.
items.answer: One morning, I woke up and floated right up off my bed. First, I flew out the window and soared over my whole neighborhood, looking down at the tiny houses and trees. Then, I flew to school and landed in the playground, and everyone cheered. Finally, when the sun set I floated back down, and I crawled into bed wishing the magic would last forever.

steps: Sentence 1: beginning with how the flying started.
Sentences 2-3: two events (where you flew, what happened).
Sentence 4: ending with a feeling.

items.prompt:
Evaluate this narrative for its beginning, middle, end, details, and temporal words. Then explain what a full score would look like.

'One day, I went to the zoo. I saw animals. I went home.'
items.answer: The narrative has a beginning ('One day, I went to the zoo'), a vague middle ('I saw animals'), and an abrupt end ('I went home'). It is missing details, temporal words, and a meaningful closing. A full-score narrative would be: 'One day, my family took me to the zoo for my birthday. First, we visited the giraffe area and I fed one a leaf from my hand. Then, we watched the penguins swim and splash. Finally, we shared ice cream by the exit, and I said it was the best birthday I had ever had.'

steps: Identify what is present: beginning and basic events.
Identify what is missing: details, temporal words, feeling at the end.
Write an improved version with all five elements.

items.prompt:
A student wrote a narrative that jumps from the beginning right to the end with no middle. Write a middle section for this story:

'One morning, I found a note on my pillow. ... I ran to tell my parents the amazing news.'
items.answer: Middle: 'First, I picked up the note and read it slowly. It said there was a treasure chest hidden in the backyard. I jumped out of bed and ran downstairs as fast as I could. Then, I searched behind every flower and bush until I found a wooden box with my name on it. Inside were my favorite snacks, a new book, and a letter from Grandma saying she loved me.'

steps: The middle should fill in what happened between finding the note and telling the parents.
Include actions in sequence with temporal words.
Build toward the amazing news so the ending makes sense.

items.prompt: Write a 4-sentence narrative about an experience at school. Include a beginning, two specific events, and a closing that shows what you learned or how you felt.
items.answer: One Thursday, my teacher surprised us by bringing a real snake to science class. First, she showed us how the snake moved without legs by using its muscles. Then, she let each student hold it, and I was nervous but I held out my hand anyway. Finally, when I felt the snake's smooth scales, I realized that things that seem scary can actually be very cool.

steps: Beginning: set the scene at school.
Two events: what the teacher showed and what students did.
Closing: what was learned or felt.

items.prompt:
Compare these two endings. Which is stronger and why?

A) We drove home.
B) As we drove home, I pressed my face against the car window and watched the fireworks fade into the dark sky, already looking forward to next year.
items.answer: B is stronger because it includes a specific detail (face against the window, fireworks fading) and shows the character's feeling (looking forward to next year). Sentence A simply states an action with no emotion or imagery.

steps: A strong ending uses sensory details and shows a feeling or thought.
Sentence B gives visual detail (fireworks, dark sky) and emotion (looking forward to next year).
Sentence A is a plain action with no depth.

items.prompt: Write a 4-sentence narrative about meeting a new friend. Include a beginning, two events in the middle, and a meaningful ending.
items.answer: On the first day of school, I sat down next to a girl I had never seen before. First, I smiled and told her my name, and she smiled back and said hers was Sofia. Then, at recess, we discovered we both loved the same book series and talked the whole time. By the end of the day, I had my first new friend of the year and could not wait to see her tomorrow.

steps: Beginning: first day of school, sat next to someone new.
Event 1: introduced yourself.
Event 2: discovered something in common.
Ending: feeling of having a new friend.

items.prompt: Your narrative should match the topic. A student was asked to write about 'a time something went wrong.' She wrote: 'One day I had a great time at the beach.' Does her story match the topic? Rewrite the first two sentences so they do.
items.answer: The story does not match the topic because it describes a great time, not something going wrong. Rewritten: 'One day I went to the beach and right away things started going wrong. First, a big wave knocked me over and I swallowed a mouthful of salty water.'

steps: The prompt asks for something that went wrong.
The student's beginning describes something positive.
Rewrite to introduce a problem right away.

items.prompt: Write a 3-sentence narrative about trying something new for the first time. Use specific details and show your feelings.
items.answer: One evening, I tried surfing for the first time on a real wave at the ocean. I wobbled and fell off the board twice, and my arms felt like noodles from paddling. But when I finally stood up for three whole seconds, I screamed with joy and my dad cheered louder than anyone on the beach.

steps: Beginning: what you tried and when.
Middle: what happened (include a struggle or challenge).
Ending: the result and an emotional reaction.

items.prompt: Write a narrative in which the problem is solved by the end. Topic: a pet that escaped from its cage.
items.answer: One afternoon, I walked into my room and gasped because my hamster Biscuit was not in his cage. First, I searched under the bed and behind the bookshelf, calling his name in a quiet voice. Then, my brother lifted a pile of laundry and there was Biscuit, curled up and sleeping on a warm sweater. Finally, I gently placed him back in his cage, double-checked the latch, and promised myself I would always keep it shut tight.

steps: Beginning: establish the problem (hamster escaped).
Middle: searching actions.
End: hamster is found and the problem is solved, with a reflection.

items.prompt: What does 'sense of closure' mean in a narrative? Write an example of a closing sentence with closure and one without.
items.answer: Sense of closure means the story feels finished and the reader knows how it turned out. With closure: 'As I walked off the stage with my ribbon, I knew that all the hours of practice had been worth it.' Without closure: 'Then I went backstage.' The first shows a feeling and ties back to the effort. The second just describes a physical action with no resolution.

steps: Closure = the story feels complete.
A closing sentence WITH closure shows the result, feeling, or lesson learned.
A closing sentence WITHOUT closure just describes a next action.

items.prompt: Write a narrative about a stormy night. Include at least four sentences, two temporal words, one detail about a sound or feeling, and a closing sentence.
items.answer: One stormy night, the thunder was so loud that it shook my bedroom window. First, I pulled my blanket over my head and squeezed my eyes shut. Then, my dog jumped up on the bed and pressed against me, warm and soft. The storm raged on, but with my dog beside me I slowly stopped trembling. Finally, the rain softened to a gentle patter and I drifted off to sleep feeling safe.

steps: Beginning: a stormy night.
First event: hiding under blanket.
Then event: dog joins.
Detail: dog felt warm and soft.
Closing: storm quieted, felt safe.

items.prompt: Write a narrative where the character learns a lesson. Topic: being patient while waiting for something exciting.
items.answer: One December morning, I saw a present under the tree with my name on it and it was all I could think about. First, I tried to shake it and guess what was inside, but Mom said I had to wait until the evening. Then, the whole day felt very long and I kept watching the clock tick slowly. Finally, when evening came and I tore off the paper, I found exactly what I had hoped for, and waiting made it feel even more special.

steps: Beginning: the exciting thing is introduced.
Middle: the struggle of waiting.
Ending: the reward comes, and the lesson is clear (waiting made it better).

items.prompt: A student's narrative has a great beginning and middle but a weak ending: '...and then we drove away.' Write a strong ending that provides closure.
items.answer: Strong ending: 'As we drove away from the cabin, I pressed my nose to the cold car window and watched the lake disappear behind the trees. I did not know when we would come back, but I already knew that weekend would be one of my favorite memories forever.'

steps: The original ending just states an action (drove away).
A strong ending adds what the character saw, felt, or thought as the experience ended.
It gives the reader a sense of the story's meaning.
